prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: Reading all eight opening ballots, I move my preferred configuration from B013 (my own first place, which no colleague ranked) to B029. B029 is the one shortlisted candidate that six members ranked and four placed in their top three, and the support comes from members with different backgrounds, so it is not an artefact of one subfield. On the merits it is a well-bounded experimental achievement: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice concept removes Doppler and recoil limits while keeping a large atom number, and Ye's group pushed strontium lattice clocks to the 10^-18 regime and into many-body clock physics. Independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST) agree at that level, so this is a measurement that others reproduce and compare, which is the experimental standard I care most about. It enables tests of fundamental constants and relativistic geodesy and feeds the process to redefine the second. The attribution is clean with two names, and every member who proposed laureates for it chose the same pair.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier recognition in precision timekeeping and control of single quantum systems: Hall and Haensch (2005, frequency combs) and Wineland and Haroche (2012). A reader could see the lattice clock as an incremental refinement of ion-clock and comb technology. Other contributors (Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Schiller and ion-clock groups) are left out by a two-name credit. The redefinition of the second is still pending, so some of the practical payoff is prospective. I judge these real but not decisive, because the lattice-clock principle is distinct from what was honoured earlier.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B029 first as a clear measurement advance that opens new physics, with an uncontroversial Katori and Ye credit and stable multi-laboratory confirmation.
responses.response: I agree on the science and the attribution, and on multi-laboratory confirmation as the decisive maturity criterion. Where I would qualify his view: the argument that the clock opens new physics is still mostly prospective. Nobody has yet used it to find a violation of a fundamental constant, so I would word the citation around the demonstrated precision and the new capability, not around discoveries still to come.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B012 first because the experimental Higgs discovery was never honoured, and the proposed trio are the early proponents and long-time leaders of ATLAS and CMS.
responses.response: I do not dispute the importance of the discovery, and I come from the same experimental tradition of large collaborations. I disagree on the attribution: the trio are founders and leaders of two collaborations of several thousand people, and a prize to them would be read as crediting the discovery itself to individuals who did not make the decisive measurement. Spokespersons at the time, analysis conveners, and accelerator and detector pioneers have comparable claims. I ranked it eighth for that reason, not for the science, and I would keep it as a candidate only if the committee can agree a defensible rationale for the three names.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B018 first: the Cirac-Zoller 1995 proposal made trapped ions a concrete quantum-computing architecture, and Blatt's group realised the gates and algorithms.
responses.response: I take the theory-plus-experiment trio seriously and kept B018 as an alternative. My hesitation is the overlap with Wineland's 2012 prize and the still-open competition among qubit platforms, since scalable fault-tolerant computing has not been shown with ions or any other platform. The 2025 prize on superconducting circuits also lowers the room for a second quantum-hardware prize soon. B029 is cleaner on both counts, though I accept that B018 has stronger conceptual weight if the committee wants a quantum-information award.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B010 first, the quantum cascade laser, as a well-bounded invention with decades of replication and commercial use, and ranks B029 second.
responses.response: I respect the clarity of the QCL as an invention and note that she also supports B029, so our preferred outcomes overlap. I did not put B010 on my own ballot, so I cannot judge its attribution among Capasso, Faist and Cho as closely as the others, and I would want the committee to test whether Cho's growth contribution is credited on the same footing as the invention itself. If B029 does not hold, I would be open to hearing the case again.

uncertainties: Whether the 2005 and 2012 prizes make the committee see the lattice clock as a continuation instead of a new contribution.
Whether Hall's, Haensch's or ion-clock groups' contributions to the stability and comparison record require a broader credit than Katori and Ye.
Whether B013 (gamma-ray burst afterglows), which I ranked first and no colleague ranked, deserves a more serious hearing in later rounds or should be dropped.
How much the pending redefinition of the second should weigh on the timing of a prize.
statement.conflict_note: I rank B013 first, and B037, which touches on astroparticle observation, second. I have documented professional connections to the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+ and XL-Calibur collaborations, and my KTH group works on gamma-ray polarimetry aimed at gamma-ray bursts, so I should declare an interest in B013 and would stay out of the final decision on it if it advances. I also hold a CERN-trained experimental background that bears on B012. No specific conflict is apparent for B029, B018, B010 or the other candidates I discuss.
